channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Oil & Gas
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Coast Guard and FBI cyber teams boarded two US-bound energy tankers whose networks were compromised by foreign cyber actors — no operational disruption, and no attribution
item.category: Top Story
item.description: A joint US Coast Guard and FBI statement, reported on 16 September, confirmed that cyber teams boarded two foreign-flagged, US-bound energy tankers in the Gulf of Mexico on 21 August and 24 August. The stated purpose was to ensure the integrity of the vessels’ operational and information technology systems “following indications that the networks of both vessels were compromised”; the Coast Guard told The Record the networks were compromised by foreign cyber actors, and Rear Adm. Amy Grable, commander of Coast Guard Cyber Command, told CBS News that investigators “did find malicious cyber activity” aboard the first vessel, where the boarding lasted about four days, and SecurityWeek quotes her as saying nothing found in the inspection suggested the tanker was unsafe to operate. Her concern — IT systems connected to the systems that control propulsion and navigation — was stated as a risk, not a finding. The boarding parties combined Coast Guard law enforcement, a vessel inspector and Cyber Protection Team members with FBI Cyber Action Team operators; SecurityWeek reports that the Coast Guard’s Cyber Protection Team has carried out roughly 40 to 50 similar boardings over the past year. The first ship is VL Prosperity, a 333-metre Liberian-flagged crude supertanker that loaded at Sidi Kerir, Egypt and was bound for Galveston, Texas; its technical and safety manager is HMM Ocean Service of South Korea — the manager, not a second vessel. The second ship, boarded on 24 August, has not been named by the Coast Guard or FBI; The Wall Street Journal reported on 17 September, as relayed by The Jerusalem Post, that it is Kohaku, which was passing through the Strait of Gibraltar on its way to a Texas port to load liquefied petroleum gas. Officially there were “no reports of operational disruptions, vessel instability, physical danger to crews, or environmental impacts”, and HMM Ocean Service says VL Prosperity has been cleared for normal operations. A reported loss of communications for about 30 hours near the Strait of Gibraltar in early August, and claims that attackers reached propulsion, navigation, cargo and fuel or lube-oil systems, originate with Iran’s Mehr News Agency and are unverified, and outlets conflict on whether any engine-room detail came from a crew member; TechCrunch repeated them on 18 September as something hackers “reportedly” did, while CISA told Bloomberg that the threat actors “did not appear to have taken control of the vessels themselves”. Bloomberg also reported, as relayed by The Next Web and Cybernews, that US authorities are tracking nearly 20 vessels worldwide and have asked ships approaching US ports to notify them; that figure has not appeared in a primary DHS or Coast Guard statement. A third energy carrier, the LNG vessel Vivit Africa LNG, was reported on 18 September to be dealing with a suspected cyber incident whose cause is undetermined; on 21 September Splash247 published the crew’s own account claiming attackers controlled safety-valve and boil-off systems, which the outlet says it has not verified (see Incidents). No agency has linked that vessel to the boardings. No US agency has attributed the compromise, and no group has claimed it; the Coast Guard has not attributed it to Iran and, per SecurityWeek, is still determining whether the two incidents are connected. No new official statement or attribution had appeared by 22 September. For oil and gas operators the point is the interface rather than the ship: crude and LPG cargoes bound for US Gulf Coast terminals, and a federal cyber response that reached the berth. - Joint US Coast Guard and FBI statement, quoted by CyberScoop and The Record, with vessel and manager detail from CBS News and gCaptain, Rear Adm. Grable’s remarks via CBS News and SecurityWeek, and CISA’s comment and the nearly-20-vessels figure via Bloomberg as relayed by The Next Web and Cybernews; second vessel named by The Wall Street Journal as relayed by The Jerusalem Post, not by the agencies; propulsion and navigation manipulation claims trace to Iranian state media and are unverified - Boardings 21 and 24 Aug 2026; publicly confirmed 16 Sep 2026; second vessel named by WSJ 17 Sep 2026; Iranian-media claims repeated by TechCrunch 18 Sep 2026; Bloomberg follow-ups relayed 18–19 Sep 2026; no new official statement to 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] The Vivit Africa LNG crew now says attackers took control of safety-valve, tank-pressure and boil-off systems — a claim the outlet has not verified, and the Italian Coast Guard still records a malfunction of undetermined cause
item.category: Incident — Suspected; crew claims control of safety systems, unverified; cause officially undetermined
item.description: On 21 September Splash247 published the account the crew of Vivit Africa LNG sent to the outlet and, it says, to Korean Register, the ship’s class society. The crew claims that attackers gained temporary control of the steam-pressure and safety-valve systems while the ship transited the Strait of Gibraltar, and later, in the Adriatic, of tank-pressure control, pressure-relief valves and boil-off gas management — which they say significantly increased the risk of tank rupture and explosion. Splash247 states plainly that it has not independently verified the claims, and no other party has confirmed them. The official record is narrower. Italian Coast Guard Capt. Roberto D’Arrigo says the master reported “a malfunction in the systems used to monitor cargo parameters” that required company technicians, that the cause “could not be identified”, and that the Coast Guard issued a navigational warning and intervened only for safety of navigation. Kongsberg Maritime, which supplies equipment aboard, said on 18 September it was too early to draw conclusions about the cause or any security implications; Vitol, the charterer, declined to comment beyond confirming the charter, and H-Line Shipping, the owner, and Korean Register have not responded. What is confirmed is the movement: the vessel loaded at Cameron LNG in Louisiana for the Adriatic LNG terminal near Rovigo, idled off Italy without discharging, then abandoned the call and sailed west toward Algeciras. Bloomberg counts it as the third tanker in about a month after the two US-bound vessels boarded by the Coast Guard and FBI, but no agency has linked the cases. Until an investigator, the class society or the equipment supplier reports, this remains a suspected incident with an unverified crew claim attached — and it is scored that way. For oil and gas the relevance is unchanged: a US LNG export cargo, and the cargo-monitoring and tank-pressure functions that are the shipboard counterpart of terminal custody-transfer, loading and ESD data. - Crew account published by Splash247, which states it has not verified it; Bloomberg report (gCaptain repost) with Italian Coast Guard, Korean Register and Kongsberg statements as quoted; vessel movements per Bloomberg and Marine Insight; cause undetermined, no attribution - Incident early Sep 2026; first reported 18 Sep 2026; crew claims published 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] CenterPoint Energy confirms customer data was taken through an external-facing system — gas and electric delivery not affected
item.category: Incident — Customer data theft at a gas and electric utility; no OT impact
item.description: CenterPoint Energy, the Houston-based electric and natural gas utility, said in an SEC filing that an unauthorised third party obtained personal information on “a portion of the Company’s customers through one of the Company’s external-facing systems.” BleepingComputer reports the system was a public API with no rate limiting, web application firewall or automated access controls. Exposed data includes names, phone numbers, service and billing addresses, account numbers, billing amounts and partial Social Security numbers. An actor using the alias “4d722e4d656f77” claims to have taken 7.49 million records and has leaked data; CenterPoint has not given a count, and class-action filings allege the intrusion ran from 17 August to 1 September. The company says electric and natural gas services were not affected, and it has notified law enforcement and regulators. This is an IT and customer-data incident, not an OT one, and it is scored that way. It belongs on an oil and gas page because gas distribution utilities run exactly this kind of customer-facing API alongside SCADA for pressure and flow — and the useful question is how much those two estates share. - CenterPoint Energy SEC filing, reported by BleepingComputer and The Record; record count claimed by the actor, not confirmed by the company - Intrusion alleged 17 Aug–1 Sep 2026; company disclosure and reporting 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] The US puts up to $10 million on the IRGC cyber commander said to direct CyberAv3ngers — energy is on the named target list
item.category: Threat Intelligence — Nation-state actor behind PLC attacks, US reward offer
item.description: On 4 September the US State Department’s Rewards for Justice programme offered up to $10 million for information on Amir Yaryab, described as a senior official of Iran’s IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command (IRGC-CEC) who leads its Cyber Operations Command. The State Department says he directs IRGC-CEC components and affiliated groups including CyberAv3ngers, Dadeh Afzar Arman and Mehrsam Andisheh Saz Nik, and that these groups have targeted critical infrastructure in the United States, Europe and the Middle East, energy and telecommunications among them. Analysis published by Security Boulevard on 9 September also names the Shahid Hemmat and Shahid Shushtari components, and ties Iran-linked groups to attacks on municipal water systems in at least 12 US states this year. The technical background is the joint CISA and FBI warning updated on 22–23 July, which said Iran-affiliated actors attacking PLCs in water and energy had widened their target set beyond Rockwell/Allen-Bradley to Schneider Modicon M340/BMX P34 and Siemens S7-1200 controllers. Those are the controller families found in wellsite automation, compressor stations, tank farms and terminal loading systems. The reward is a policy step, not a new intrusion, and the attributions are US government assessments. - US State Department Rewards for Justice announcement, reported by RFE/RL via GlobalSecurity and analysed by Security Boulevard; technical background from the CISA/FBI update reported by Cybersecurity Dive - Reward announced 4 Sep 2026; analysis 9 Sep 2026; joint advisory updated 22–23 Jul 2026

item.title: [High] Red Heron broke into self-hosted Gitea and walked out with SCADA and HMI source code from an industrial automation vendor
item.category: Threat Intelligence — PRC-linked campaign, SCADA/HMI source code theft
item.description: Acronis’ Threat Research Unit published findings on 13 September, reported on 14–15 September, on a campaign it attributes with moderate confidence to Red Heron, a Chinese-speaking, PRC-linked actor, exploiting CVE-2026-60004, the CVSS 9.8 Gitea remote code execution flaw fixed in Gitea 1.27.1 on 27 July. Acronis confirms 11 compromised targets across Canada, Argentina, Taiwan, the United States and Sri Lanka, including a Canadian renewable energy company, a Taiwanese industrial automation firm, municipal platforms and defence, aerospace and telecoms organisations. From the automation firm the attackers took the source code of a SCADA/HMI tool used in industrial control environments, along with IoT integrations and a network sniffer; “hundreds of repositories” were exfiltrated from a single target. The tooling includes the JITTERLY implant, with more than 30 post-exploitation commands, and a previously undocumented Linux rootkit Acronis calls SIXZUT. No oil or gas victim has been reported. The relevance is twofold: stolen HMI source gives an attacker a head start on finding flaws in products that end up in process plants, and O&G engineering teams and integrators increasingly keep PLC logic, HMI projects and SIS configuration in exactly this kind of self-hosted Git server. - Acronis Threat Research Unit research, reported by Industrial Cyber; victims unnamed, attribution moderate confidence - Acronis research 13 Sep 2026; reporting 14–15 Sep 2026; Gitea flaw in KEV since 25 Aug 2026 (due 28 Aug, passed)

item.title: [Medium] August set a global ransomware record at 997 attacks — energy incidents so far are landing on IT, and that is where the outage comes from
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Ransomware statistics
item.description: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — about 32 a day, a 23 percent rise on July’s 809 and above the previous monthly record of 988 in February 2025. Attacks on businesses reached 861 and on healthcare 69, while attacks on utilities doubled from five to ten. Qilin, with 157 claims, and The Gentlemen, with 107, together accounted for more than a quarter of the total. Treat the absolute numbers with caution: counts of this kind rest largely on leak-site claims and disclosure practice, and a claimed victim is not a confirmed one. The data does not break out oil and gas. The pattern it fits is nonetheless the one the sector already knows from Colonial Pipeline onward — encryption lands on business systems, and operations stop because scheduling, billing, custody-transfer accounting or terminal ticketing depends on them, not because anything touched a controller. - Comparitech monthly ransomware tracking, reported by Industrial Cyber; counts largely based on actor claims and do not break out oil and gas - Data for August 2026; reporting published 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Nozomi chains 12 flaws in the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 to root on an OT edge device — patched, and not exploited
item.category: Research — OT edge device, vendor-patched vulnerability chain
item.description: Nozomi Networks Labs published the second part of its Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 research on 18 September: twelve vulnerabilities in total, nine in the device firmware and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client. Firmware below V4.0 HF0 and Edge Client releases through V2.1 are affected, and Siemens has published an advisory with fixes in V4.0 HF0 and later. Nozomi demonstrated that several of the flaws can be chained to obtain root-level control of the device, which would allow manipulation of telemetry, suppression of alarms, access to operational data, disruption of edge services and lateral movement into the networks the device sits between. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. Two dates are worth keeping apart: CISA updated the long-standing advisory ICSA-25-135-18 on 15 September to add the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client and the vendor fixes — an advisory update, not a new vulnerability — and this 18 September publication is the research behind it. The CVE identifiers in this set carry 2025 prefixes despite the 2026 disclosure, which is consistent with how the line was assigned but worth confirming against Siemens’ own advisory before you put them in a ticket. Our sector read: local processing engines and SINEMA remote access are used for edge processing and vendor connectivity at remote and unmanned sites, which is where root on an edge box buys the most. - Nozomi Networks Labs research reported by Industrial Cyber, with the related CISA advisory update to ICSA-25-135-18 of 15 Sep 2026; CVE identifiers to be confirmed against the Siemens advisory - Research published 18 Sep 2026; related CISA advisory update 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A hard-coded key and MD5 password hashes inside AVEVA Pipeline Integrity Monitor — read access to the project files is enough
item.category: Critical Advisory — Pipeline leak detection and integrity monitoring
item.description: CISA published advisory ICSA-26-253-01 on 10 September covering four vulnerabilities in the PIMBoards component of AVEVA Pipeline Integrity Monitor, AVEVA’s real-time leak-detection and integrity product for liquid and gas pipelines. All versions up to and including 2025 SP1 P1 are affected. CVE-2026-81821, a hard-coded cryptographic key (CVSS v3 8.4), lets anyone who can read PIMBoards project files decrypt the sensitive information inside them. CVE-2026-81822, weak MD5 password hashing (CVSS v3 8.4), exposes password hashes to brute force and a potential route to administrator access. CVE-2026-81823, missing authorisation (5.3), allows unauthorised reads of PIMBoards data, and CVE-2026-81824, a cross-site scripting flaw (4.7), lets a malicious link run script in a user’s session. AVEVA found the first two itself; researcher Adham Khairy Ramadan reported the others. The fix is the 2025 SP1 P2 security update, and AVEVA notes that migrating legacy project files to the new cryptography is one-way. No exploitation has been reported. This is the most directly pipeline-specific advisory of the period: whoever can read or administer PIM can see, and potentially change, the leak-detection configuration and dashboards that controllers rely on for safety decisions. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-253-01 and AVEVA security bulletin, reported by ISSSource and SecurityWeek - Advisory published 10 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Schneider fixes a CVSS 9.2 authentication flaw in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety — and SCADAPack RTUs are in the same release
item.category: Critical Advisory — Process and safety controller authentication
item.description: Schneider Electric’s September Patch Tuesday release on 8 September included SEVD-2026-251-04 for CVE-2026-3869, an incorrect implementation of an authentication algorithm (CWE-303) scored CVSS v4.0 9.2. The weakness is exposed when a project built at a lower application level runs, and can affect confidentiality, integrity and availability. Affected are Modicon M580 at application levels below 4.00 and Modicon M580 Safety below 4.20; Blastwave’s analysis says Modicon MC80 is also affected. The same release fixed a medium-severity defect in SCADAPack x70 RTUs and a high-severity issue in PowerLogic T300, and updated four existing advisories. Nothing in the release is reported as exploited. The sector relevance is our assessment rather than the vendor’s: M580 and M580 Safety controllers run process and safety functions in gas processing, terminals and refinery units, and SCADAPack RTUs are a common choice for wellsite automation and pipeline telemetry. An authentication weakness in a safety-rated controller is the kind of finding that belongs in the SIS change process, not the general patch queue. - Schneider Electric security notice SEVD-2026-251-04, with analysis from Blastwave and the September Patch Tuesday round-up in SecurityWeek; oil and gas applicability is editorial assessment - Released 8 Sep 2026 (September ICS Patch Tuesday)

item.title: [Critical] A cluster with Sandworm-overlapping tooling and a Qilin ransomware affiliate got into Cisco firewall management consoles — the consoles that set your IT/OT boundary rules
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited firewall management platform, CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is being exploited in the wild. It is a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass: a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the appliance. CISA added it to KEV the same day with a federal remediation deadline of 12 September, now passed. Cisco Talos describes three post-compromise clusters. UAT-12197 used CVE-2026-20079 and is not attributed to a named actor. UAT-11823, an APT whose tooling overlaps with the Russian group Sandworm, used CVE-2026-20079 together with CVE-2026-20316 and deployed a variant of Cyclops Blink — Talos does not say Sandworm itself was responsible. UAT-11988, which Talos assesses with high confidence is a ransomware operator with TTPs consistent with Qilin affiliates, got in only through CVE-2026-20316, a CVSS 5.3 static-credential flaw that is not in KEV, and ultimately deployed Qilin. On 16 September Cisco published its hardening release, cisco-sa-hardening-asaftdfmc-uvpPROhN, covering eight internally found flaws across ASA, FTD and FMC (CVE-2026-20329 to CVE-2026-20336, maximum CVSS 9.9); it accompanies the exploited FMC flaws. No OT impact and no oil and gas victim has been named. But FMC is where the firewall policy between corporate networks and plant, pipeline SCADA and terminal control networks is written, so root on FMC is the ability to quietly loosen that boundary. - Cisco security advisory update and Cisco Talos research of 9 Sep 2026, plus the CISA KEV addition — reported by SecurityWeek, cluster detail corroborated by The Hacker News - Advisory updated and KEV listing added 9 Sep 2026; reporting 10 Sep 2026; federal deadline 12 Sep 2026; hardening release 16 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in SonicWall’s SMA1000 remote-access gateway is being exploited — and CISA says patching alone does not close it
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited remote-access gateway, KEV-listed
item.description: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway are being exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-83548, scored CVSS 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface; CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an operating-system command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console. Chained, they give an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution on the appliance. CISA added both to KEV on 2 September with a 5 September federal deadline and flagged both for forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 — a signal that patching does not end the incident. Affected models are the SMA1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v; SSL-VPN on SonicWall firewalls and the SMA 100 series are not affected. Remote-access gateways like this are how automation vendors, integrators and on-call engineers reach DCS, SCADA and terminal systems out of hours, which makes the appliance a boundary device whether or not it is inventoried as one. - SonicWall PSIRT advisory and CISA KEV addition of 2 Sep 2026 — reported by BleepingComputer, corroborated by SecurityWeek and Help Net Security - Vendor advisory 1 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 2 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] CISA’s 8 September KEV batch is led by a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in the RMM platform your managed-service provider may use
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited RMM platform, KEV-listed
item.description: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 8 September, all with vendor fixes available. The one that matters most for oil and gas operations is CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, scored CVSS 10.0: a static code injection weakness giving pre-authentication remote code execution on the remote monitoring and management server. N-able has confirmed exploitation in the wild, Huntress reported attacks against N-central’s API from 4 September, and N-able shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — its fourth hotfix in five weeks. The federal deadline of 11 September has passed. RMM agents run with high privilege on the hosts they manage, and at smaller producers, midstream gathering operators and fuel distributors, IT is frequently outsourced to an MSP whose agents sit on the same Windows servers that host historians, SCADA clients or terminal automation. The batch also carries two exploited Windows privilege-escalation zero-days, CVE-2026-81963 in the Update Stack and CVE-2026-85880 in ALPC, both giving SYSTEM, plus an Adobe Commerce template-injection flaw. - CISA KEV catalog addition of 8 Sep 2026 — corroborated by BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek and CyberScoop reporting on the N-able and Microsoft disclosures - Added to KEV 8 Sep 2026; N-able hotfix released 5 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA adds five exploited flaws to KEV, including ScreenConnect — the remote-support tool that turns up on vendor-supplied OT PCs
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited remote-support and build tooling
item.description: CISA added five vulnerabilities affecting JFrog Artifactory, ConnectWise ScreenConnect and MikroTik RouterOS to the KEV catalog on 12 September on evidence of active exploitation, with federal remediation deadlines of 13 September for RouterOS, 14 September for ScreenConnect and 25 September for Artifactory. Reporting indicates the Artifactory flaws were chained to gain administrator control, establish persistence and install Rust-based backdoors; ScreenConnect exploitation reportedly enabled unauthorised file transfer and execution through active sessions using a malicious VBScript payload; and the RouterOS entry reflects the CERT Polska chain covered separately on this page. No oil and gas victim is named. The ScreenConnect entry is the one to read twice: remote-support tools are how OEM service desks and integrators reach compressor-control panels, analyser shelters, terminal automation PCs and engineering workstations, and they are often installed by the vendor rather than by the operator’s own security team. - CISA KEV catalog addition — reported by The Hacker News - KEV addition 12 Sep 2026; reporting 13 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] “MikroTrick” is now confirmed exploited — two CVSS 9.2 SSH flaws hand over RouterOS admin on the routers at remote sites
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, remote-site edge routers
item.description: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS chain known as “MikroTrick”, disclosed earlier but not previously confirmed as exploited, is being used in real-world attacks observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs an SSH authentication bypass, CVE-2026-67276 at CVSS 9.2, with an SSH privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-86060 at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device. A third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure or denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. CISA added the exploited flaws to KEV on 12 September. CERT Polska named no victims or sectors, only that MikroTik devices are widely deployed by ISPs, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks, so there is no confirmed oil and gas victim. It earns its place here because inexpensive, capable routers are a common contractor choice for cellular and fixed-wireless backhaul at wellpads, tank batteries, remote valve and meter stations — often the one device on site with a route to both the SCADA host and the internet. - CERT Polska alert — reported by Industrial Cyber; CISA KEV addition 12 Sep 2026. No victims or sectors named - Exploitation observed from 2 Sep 2026; CERT Polska confirmation 9 Sep 2026; KEV listing 12 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA adds Zyxel GS1900 switches to KEV after one actor pulled configs and root credentials from nearly a thousand of them — the switch class that turns up at small stations and contractor sites
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited small-site managed switch, CISA KEV
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 21 September with a federal remediation deadline of 24 September. It is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel’s GS1900-series managed switches — GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2 — that lets an unauthenticated attacker with access to the management interface run operating-system commands through a crafted HTTP request. Zyxel patched it on 16 June in firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and the per-model equivalents, and gives no CVSS score, so we print none. GreyNoise’s report of the same day describes what it calls the first observed in-the-wild exploitation: a single actor, active since 7 May and assessed by GreyNoise to be a Chinese speaker, compromised 996 GS1900 switches in 48 countries — Italy, the United States and Taiwan the largest shares — using an obfuscated Python tool that pulled device configurations and root-level password hashes over TFTP. GreyNoise says 564 of the victims were still on factory-default credentials. The same actor stole records from an unnamed western government organisation through two WordPress flaws and probed Gitea, UniFi, Proxmox and PAN-OS GlobalProtect; GreyNoise infers overlap with Red Heron from shared infrastructure and malware, which is an inference rather than an observation. No oil and gas victim is named and no OT impact is reported. The sector read is ours: GS1900 is an inexpensive managed switch, not industrial-rated, and it is exactly what a contractor or a small operator installs in a wellsite shelter, a meter station cabinet or a terminal office to hang cellular routers, cameras and an HMI PC off — the places where a device configuration in an attacker’s hands maps your remote-site network for them. - CISA KEV catalog addition (21 Sep 2026), Zyxel security advisory (16 Jun 2026) and GreyNoise research (21 Sep 2026); actor language and Red Heron overlap are GreyNoise assessments and inferences; oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment - Zyxel fix 16 Jun 2026; GreyNoise report and KEV addition 21 Sep 2026; federal deadline 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Dutch NCSC warns exploitation of two CVSS 9.8 Check Point VPN flaws is imminent — patches landed 9 September
item.category: Critical Advisory — VPN gateway, exploitation assessed imminent
item.description: The Netherlands’ National Cyber Security Centre issued a warning, reported on 12 September, that it expects near-term exploitation of two critical vulnerabilities in Check Point VPN products, CVE-2026-85102 and CVE-2026-85103, both carrying CVSS 9.8 in reporting. The pair can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on Security Gateways, and a certificate-decoding defect can also affect Security Management Servers. Check Point released fixes on 9 September. No public proof-of-concept had been reported and no exploitation confirmed at the time of the warning — the NCSC’s position is a forecast, not an observation. Firewall and VPN gateways of this class commonly sit at the IT/OT boundary of refineries, gas plants and pipeline control centres, where they often terminate the vendor and contractor tunnels into those networks. - Dutch National Cyber Security Centre warning — reported by BleepingComputer; exploitation assessed as imminent, not confirmed - Check Point fixes 9 Sep 2026; NCSC warning reported 12 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Check Point fixes a CVSS 9.8 pre-authentication root flaw in the servers that write your firewall policy — no exploitation reported
item.category: Critical Advisory — Firewall management server, pre-authentication RCE, not exploited
item.description: Check Point has fixed CVE-2026-91843, rated CVSS 9.8, in its Security Management and Log Servers, under advisory sk1000155, as reported by The Hacker News on 17 September and in SecurityWeek’s round-up. A stack overflow in the login process, triggered by an overly long username in an unauthenticated request, can give a remote attacker code execution as root. The Hacker News reports that a Trusted Clients misconfiguration is a precondition; that detail could not be confirmed in the vendor text, so check sk1000155 against your own configuration rather than relying on it. Reported affected versions are R82.10 up to Jumbo Hotfix Take 44, R82 up to Take 126, all builds of R82.20, R81.20 up to Take 166, R81.10 up to Take 190, and the end-of-support R81 and R80.x lines; Multi-Domain Server is affected and Smart-1 Cloud is already fixed. The fix is a LivePatch delivered through sk1000155. Check Point says there is “no indication that this vulnerability has been exploited in the wild.” This is separate from the VPN flaws the Dutch NCSC warned about on 12 September. The management server is where policy for the gateways at the IT/OT boundary of refineries, gas plants and pipeline control centres is written, so root on it is the ability to change that boundary everywhere at once. - Check Point advisory sk1000155, as reported by The Hacker News and SecurityWeek; the vendor page itself was not directly reviewed - Reported 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] September ICS Patch Tuesday: Siemens ships nine advisories and starts fixing the “Copy Fail” Linux kernel flaw across its product lines
item.category: Critical Advisory — September ICS Patch Tuesday round-up
item.description: Siemens published nine new advisories and updated nine existing ones in the 8 September ICS patch round. The critical-severity findings are in the Reyrolle 7SR5 relay family, Open Interface Services, Industrial Edge Management and SIMOVE Fleetmanager/SIPLANT; Desigo CC, Teamcenter, the Mendix SAML module and Element Maps received high-severity fixes. Siemens also began shipping updates across affected products for the Linux kernel “Copy Fail” vulnerability, CVE-2026-31431 at CVSS 7.8, which can give a local attacker a root shell. In the same cycle Schneider Electric fixed the Modicon M580 authentication flaw covered separately above, and AVEVA published the Pipeline Integrity Monitor advisory also covered above, while noting a previously disclosed medium-severity deserialisation issue in AVEVA Enterprise SCADA. Nothing in the round is reported as exploited. Most of Siemens’ items are grid, building or edge products rather than oil and gas specific, but Industrial Edge and embedded Linux devices appear in upstream and refinery digitalisation projects, and AVEVA Enterprise SCADA is widely used for pipeline control. - Siemens ProductCERT, Schneider Electric and AVEVA security advisories of 8 Sep 2026 — summarised by SecurityWeek - Advisories published 8 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Rockwell revises its lock-out recovery notice a fifth time, adding Micro820 and Micro850 — the small controllers at wellsites and pump skids that attackers have been setting passwords on
item.category: Critical Advisory — Vendor hardening notice, revised after attackers locked operators out of exposed PLCs
item.description: Rockwell Automation published revision 5.0 of security notice SD1790, “Important Hardening Guidance for Rockwell Automation/Allen-Bradley Controllers and Instructions for Restoring Access When the Password Is Unknown”, on 18 September. First issued on 30 July alongside an FBI public service announcement, the notice describes threat actors remotely altering the configuration of internet-exposed programmable logic controllers, changing their IP addresses and setting passwords where none existed, so that operators lose access to their own equipment. Revision 2.0 added MicroLogix 1100 recovery steps in July; revision 4.0 in August clarified that setting a password alone is not a sufficient mitigation; revision 5.0 extends the recovery instructions and hardening guidance to Micro820 and Micro850 controllers alongside MicroLogix 1100 and 1400. There is no CVE, because there is no vulnerability: the activity works through internet exposure and missing or default credentials. The recommended actions are to remove controllers from the public internet, use a VPN for any remote access that is genuinely needed, isolate controllers behind firewalls on a separate OT network, set strong passwords and keep offline backups, monitor logs, keep firmware current and leave controllers in RUN mode so configuration cannot be changed remotely. The FBI announcement concerned water and wastewater; the sector link here is our assessment. MicroLogix and Micro800 controllers are the same low-cost class found at wellsite separators and chemical-injection skids, saltwater-disposal pumps, small compressor packages and tank-battery automation, often installed by a packager with a cellular modem and never surveyed again. Rockwell published no new product vulnerability advisories between 10 and 22 September. - Rockwell Automation security notice SD1790 revision 5.0, referencing the FBI public service announcement of 30 Jul 2026; oil and gas applicability is editorial assessment - Notice first published 30 Jul 2026; revision 5.0 published 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10 authentication bypass in Cisco ISE is being exploited — the policy engine that decides who gets onto your network
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited network access control platform, CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass in Cisco Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC. An API endpoint with insufficient authentication lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker bypass the web-based management interface. Cisco states that its PSIRT is aware of active exploitation, and all versions are affected until patched: 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4 carry the fix. There are no workarounds; Cisco points to infrastructure ACLs restricting management traffic as the only mitigation. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 16 September with a three-day federal deadline of 19 September, which has now passed. No new advisory revision has appeared; on 21 September Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency issued its own alert, AL-2026-126, urging the same patching, and ISE 3.0 is end-of-life and must be migrated rather than patched. No actor has been named, no indicators beyond checking access logs for unfamiliar usernames have been published, and no critical-infrastructure targeting has been claimed. The sector relevance is our assessment: ISE is the NAC and 802.1X policy engine that, in many operators, decides which devices and which vendor sessions are allowed onto the industrial DMZ and the plant network. Administrative control of it is administrative control of your segmentation policy. - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 and the CISA KEV catalog, reported by SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer - Advisory published 16 Sep 2026; KEV addition 16 Sep 2026, deadline 19 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A crafted email is enough: Cisco Secure Email Gateway SQL injection exploited as a zero-day, root without user interaction
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited email gateway, CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco advisory cisco-sa-esa-inj-2bLVGmhX, first published 14 September, covers CVE-2026-76461, a CVSS 9.8 SQL-injection flaw in AsyncOS email parsing on Cisco Secure Email Gateway. An unauthenticated attacker who sends a specially crafted email can run arbitrary SQL and then commands as root, with no user interaction and regardless of appliance configuration; physical and virtual appliances are both affected. Cisco says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in September 2026. Fixed builds are available, with 16.5.0-780 the preferred target and separate fixed builds for the 16.0 and 15.5 trains — outlets have printed inconsistent build strings, so take yours from the Cisco advisory. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 14 September with a federal deadline of 17 September, now passed. Shadowserver counted more than 400 exposed appliances. No attribution has been published and no industrial targeting has been reported. This is an IT mail gateway, not an OT device, and we list it for one reason: it is an unauthenticated, no-click path to root inside the enterprise that hosts your engineering workstations, historians and remote-access brokers. - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-esa-inj-2bLVGmhX and the CISA KEV catalog, reported by BleepingComputer, Help Net Security and Cybersecurity Dive - Advisory published and KEV addition 14 Sep 2026; federal deadline 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] mySCADA myPRO Manager hands privileged management functions to anyone who can reach it — CVSS 9.8, fixed in 2.2
item.category: Critical Advisory — HMI/SCADA management server for remote sites
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-258-03, published 15 September, covers two flaws in mySCADA myPRO Manager. CVE-2026-73807, CVSS v3 9.8, is a missing-authorisation flaw in the command API: an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the interface gets privileged management functions. CVE-2026-82567, CVSS 6.3 and adjacent-network only, allows unauthenticated sending of arbitrary SMS messages through a connected GSM modem. Versions up to and including 2.1 are affected; 2.2 is the fix. CISA lists Energy among the affected sectors, alongside Water and Wastewater, Critical Manufacturing, Food and Agriculture and Transportation, and states that no public exploitation targeting these flaws has been reported to it. The sector read is ours: myPRO is an inexpensive HMI and SCADA package that turns up at small and unmanned sites — gathering systems, small gas plants, tank farms and contractor-supplied skids — typically behind a cellular router with SMS alerting attached. Those are exactly the deployments least likely to appear in a corporate asset register. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-258-03; oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment - Advisory published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] CISA republishes the SCADAPack x70 credential flaw — the RTU family at wellheads, metering runs and compressor stations
item.category: Critical Advisory — Wellsite, pipeline and station RTUs
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-258-04, published 15 September, republishes Schneider Electric’s 8 September notice SEVD-2026-251-03 and gives the flaw an identifier: CVE-2026-81861, CVSS v3 6.5 (v4 5.9), insufficiently protected credentials in the Secure Lock function. The consequence is unauthorised access to RTU configuration. The advisory lists SCADAPack 47x, 47xi, 47xd, 470R and 57x, with the product tree also naming SCADAPack 3xx and 32; CISA records the affected sectors as Critical Manufacturing and Energy. No code fix is listed in CISA’s machine-readable advisory — the remedies are configuration: enable role-based access control as set out in Schneider’s SCADAPack security guidelines, segment the RTU networks, and use the RTU Firewall Service to restrict which services are reachable. No exploitation has been reported. This is the CVE detail behind the SCADAPack line in Schneider’s September release, and it matters here more than the score suggests: these are the remote units that report and control at unmanned sites, often over cellular or licensed radio, where “who can read the configuration” is not a theoretical question. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-258-04, republishing Schneider Electric security notification SEVD-2026-251-03; sector applicability is editorial assessment - Schneider notice 8 Sep 2026; CISA advisory published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] About 20 flaws in one shared IO-Link master firmware base hit three vendors at once — unauthenticated root at the field layer
item.category: Critical Advisory — Field-layer I/O, shared OEM firmware
item.description: CERT@VDE published three advisories on 16 September that carry the same CVE range, CVE-2026-27546 through CVE-2026-27565, across three different brands: VDE-2026-014 for Pepperl+Fuchs ICE2-* and ICE3-* models, VDE-2026-027 for Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 EIP DI8 and IOL MA8 PN DI8, and VDE-2026-028 for Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 units. One shared CVE set across three vendors points to a common OEM firmware base. The worst two are CVE-2026-27546, an authentication bypass at CVSS 9.8, and CVE-2026-27565, an OS command injection at CVSS 9.8 reachable over the network without authentication or user interaction; below them sit command-injection and local-file-inclusion flaws at 8.8, an authorisation bypass at 8.1, path traversal at 7.5 and information disclosure at 6.5. The outcome is unauthenticated root code execution on the device and theft of stored password hashes and SSH private keys. Firmware below 1.7.4 is affected and the advisories name 1.7.8 as fixed — confirm the exact build with your vendor. No exploitation has been reported. IO-Link masters aggregate sensors and actuators onto EtherNet/IP and PROFINET segments; in oil and gas they usually arrive inside packaged equipment — metering and analyser cabinets, custody-transfer skids, vendor process packages — rather than in the main DCS I/O count, which is why they are easy to miss. - CERT@VDE advisories VDE-2026-014, VDE-2026-027 and VDE-2026-028; oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment - Advisories published 16 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Seven new CISA ICS advisories plus one update on 17 September — Hitachi Energy FACTS, three Schneider products, Mitsubishi GX Works3, ABB Edgenius and an ELD
item.category: Critical Advisory — CISA ICS advisory batch
item.description: CISA released eight ICS advisories on Thursday 17 September — seven new, ICSA-26-260-01 through -07, plus one update: Bransys ELD, Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings, Hitachi Energy FACTS Control Platform, Schneider Electric Modicon M340 controllers and communication modules, Schneider Electric NetBotz 5 (750 and 755), ABB Ability Edgenius, and Schneider Electric PowerChute Serial Shutdown. GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings carry CVE-2026-15688, an authentication algorithm flaw scored CVSS v3.1 8.8 and v4.0 8.7, affecting all versions and enabling local authentication bypass and tampering with control programs. The Bransys electronic logging device has three hardcoded or cleartext credential flaws — CVE-2026-86520 (7.5), CVE-2026-86689 (5.9) and CVE-2026-77960 (5.3) — fixed in Android 11.00.00 and iOS 1.1.54. CISA’s machine-readable files now confirm four more. Modicon M340 and its X80 Ethernet modules (-04) carry CVE-2025-6625, a crafted-FTP-command denial of service scored CVSS v3.1 7.5 and v4.0 8.7, fixed from M340 firmware SV3.70 (with BMXNOE0100 3.60, BMXNOE0110 6.80 and BMXNOR0200H SV1.7_IR27 for the modules); it republishes a Schneider advisory first issued in August 2025, so the CVE year is not a typo. NetBotz 5, PowerChute and Edgenius are likewise republications of vendor advisories originally dated 11 August and 25 June. NetBotz 5 (-05) has an OS command injection, CVE-2026-13336 (v3.1 6.4, v4.0 7.3), plus CVE-2026-13337, fixed in 5.6.0. ABB Ability Edgenius (-06) inherits the Linux kernel “Copy Fail” privilege escalation, CVE-2026-31431 (7.8), fixed in 3.2.4.1. PowerChute Serial Shutdown (-07) has CVE-2026-13348, weak limits on authentication attempts (v3.1 5.3, v4.0 6.9), with version 1.6 as Schneider’s remediation. The Hitachi Energy advisory (-03) is not yet in the mirror; per reporting on Hitachi Energy advisory 8DBD000229, it covers CVE-2024-4872 and CVE-2024-3980 (CVSS 9.9), CVE-2024-3982 (8.2), CVE-2024-7940 (8.3, a service exposed without authentication) and CVE-2024-7941 (4.3) in FACTS Control Platform 3.4.0 to 4.1.1 where the GWS component is installed — see that advisory for remediation. CISA also updated ICSA-26-211-07, the Mitsubishi CC-Link IE TSN advisory, on 17 September, adding eight affected products. No exploitation is reported for anything in the batch, and none of its CVEs are in KEV; CISA’s KEV additions in the period were three Linux kernel flaws on 18 September (federal deadline 21 September, passed) and a Zyxel GS1900 switch flaw on 21 September, covered separately. No 22 September ICS batch had been published at generation time. The two worth an oil and gas look are Modicon M340, a controller family common in utilities and balance-of-plant duties, and Edgenius, an industrial edge platform — judge both against your own estate rather than the sector labels. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-260-01 through -07 plus update ICSA-26-211-07 (17 Sep 2026); detail for -01 and -04 to -07 confirmed from CISA’s CSAF files, -02 from the advisory page, and Hitachi -03 CVEs per ISSSource reporting on Hitachi Energy advisory 8DBD000229 - Advisories published 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] ABB Freelance DCS controllers can be stopped by one crafted, unauthenticated network message — the fixes are already in shipped update rollups
item.category: Critical Advisory — Process DCS controller denial of service
item.description: ABB published advisory 7PAA010706 on 18 September for CVE-2023-5778, a missing length check in its Freelance distributed control system. An attacker with network access to an affected controller can send a specially crafted message that makes it stop; no credentials are needed. ABB scores it CVSS v3.1 7.5 (availability impact only). Affected are Freelance DCP, AC 700F, AC 800F and AC 900F controllers on Freelance 2013 and earlier, 2013 SP1, 2016, 2016 SP1, 2019 and 2019 SP1. The fixes already exist in Freelance 2013 SP1 RU06, 2016 SP1 RU07, 2019 SP1 RU03 and later rollups, 2019 SP1 FP1, and Freelance 2024, which is not affected. For AC 700F and AC 900F on Freelance 2016 and later, turning on Download-Protection from the Display Unit blocks the attack. ABB says the flaw had not been publicly disclosed or exploited when it issued the advisory. The sector link is our assessment, not ABB’s: Freelance runs process control in gas processing, compression, tank farms and smaller process plants, and many of those sites stay on older releases that never took the later rollups. - ABB cybersecurity advisory 7PAA010706 (CSAF), CVE-2023-5778; oil and gas applicability is editorial assessment - Advisory published 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Moxa TN-4500B switches can be knocked over by an over-long username at the web login — CVSS 8.8, fixed in firmware 2.1
item.category: Critical Advisory — Industrial Ethernet switch, unauthenticated denial of service
item.description: Moxa published advisory MPSA-252620 on 18 September for CVE-2026-15579 in its TN-4500B series Ethernet switches. Improper validation of the username field at web login lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker send an excessively long value that overflows a buffer and crashes the authentication process, producing a denial of service; Moxa scores it CVSS v4.0 8.8 with a network attack vector, no privileges and no user interaction, with high impact on availability and low impact on integrity. Firmware 2.0 and earlier is affected and 2.1 or later is the fix. Moxa credits researcher Mask Lu and reports no exploitation. Where an immediate update is not possible, Moxa’s mitigations are the usual ones: firewall the management interface, segregate operational networks with VLANs, disable unused services, use multi-factor authentication and strong passwords, and enable logging and monitoring. Be honest about fit before you act: the TN series is Moxa’s rolling-stock and vehicle-rated switch line, built for railway use, so it appears in oil and gas only where someone specified a vehicle-grade, wide-temperature switch — mobile or skid-mounted units and some offshore or vibration-heavy installations. If your register has none, the useful residue is the pattern: a management-plane crash on a switch that carries control traffic is an availability event for whatever sits behind it, so the reachability of switch web logins from anything other than a named engineering segment is worth confirming across your whole switch estate, Moxa or not. - Moxa security advisory MPSA-252620, CVE-2026-15579; oil and gas applicability is editorial assessment and is limited - Advisory published 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] The Coast Guard now has one office that owns maritime cyber policy — relevant to every waterfront oil and LNG terminal it regulates
item.category: Regulation — US Coast Guard maritime cyber governance
item.description: The US Coast Guard has established the Office of Maritime Cybersecurity Policy (CG-MCP) under its Director of Inspections and Compliance, as the central authority for cybersecurity policy across the Marine Transportation System. Its remit is to develop domestic policy, contribute to international standards, direct a unified compliance and enforcement strategy, and serve as the main point of contact for industry. The move follows Government Accountability Office findings on gaps in Coast Guard cyber oversight, including weak incident tracking and missing personnel competency standards. Nothing in the maritime cyber rule changes today. The relevance to oil and gas is that the Coast Guard is the security regulator for waterfront facilities handling crude, refined products and LNG, and it was Coast Guard cyber teams, with the FBI, that boarded the US-bound tankers in the top story. Consolidating policy and compliance under one office usually means the same questions, asked the same way, at more facilities. - US Coast Guard announcement — reported by SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber - Office establishment reported 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] 117 federal reporting rules across 27 agencies — and the first hours of a pipeline incident are when they collide
item.category: Policy — Federal incident reporting
item.description: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce published analysis on 8 September, drawing on Government Accountability Office work, counting 117 separate federal cyber incident reporting regulations spread across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. Their argument is operational: duplicative notifications with different thresholds, formats and clocks pull the same small group of people away from containment during the hours when containment matters most. Oil and gas operators will recognise the shape. A single cyber event can touch TSA’s pipeline security directive reporting to CISA, Coast Guard reporting for marine terminals, SEC disclosure for listed companies, state regulators, cyber insurers and contractual notice to shippers and customers. The analysis lands as the CIRCIA rules are expected to be finalised this autumn, which is when harmonisation either happens or does not. - McCrary Institute and US Chamber of Commerce analysis citing GAO data, reported by Industrial Cyber - Published 8 Sep 2026; CIRCIA final rule expected autumn 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA’s cyber decoys guide: tripwires and honeytokens as detection you can add without touching production
item.category: Guidance — Detection engineering for critical infrastructure
item.description: CISA published “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September. The guide defines decoys as assets that appear to be legitimate systems, accounts or data but exist to distract adversaries, detect their presence or support intelligence collection, and it structures deployment in three phases: preparation, execution and analysis. CISA positions decoys alongside Zero Trust rather than as a replacement for either segmentation or monitoring. The reason it is worth an oil and gas reader’s time is the constraint it fits: most detection improvements in OT require touching a production system, and decoys mostly do not. A fake engineering workstation credential that no legitimate process uses, a planted project file, a dormant account named to look like a vendor login — each of these produces a signal with a very low false-positive rate and no change to the control system itself. That makes it one of the few detection moves that can be made between turnarounds rather than during one. - CISA guidance “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response”, reported by SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber; OT applicability is editorial assessment - Guidance published 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA retires its weekly vulnerability bulletin on 28 September — if your patch triage consumes it, change the input now
item.category: Policy — Federal vulnerability information sources
item.description: CISA is discontinuing its weekly Vulnerability Summary bulletin with effect from 28 September 2026, reported on 17 September. The agency is pointing users instead to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, its alerts and its advisories, and frames the change as consistent with the risk-based prioritisation set out in BOD 26-04 of June 2026. Nothing in the reporting indicates that ICS advisories are affected, and the KEV catalog continues unchanged. The practical point for operators is narrow but real: the weekly bulletin is a bulk feed that several vulnerability-management workflows and vendor summaries quietly depend on, and a feed that simply stops publishing tends to fail silently rather than loudly. If your process has a step that begins “each week, review the CISA vulnerability summary”, that step needs a new source before the end of the month. - Reported by SecurityWeek; CISA continues the KEV catalog, alerts and advisories - Announced 17 Sep 2026; effective 28 Sep 2026
